paragraphs: Long robotic tasks require both a useful plan and the physical ability to carry it out. This paper separates those responsibilities to support generalization to unseen tasks from one example. Its central idea is to generate a trajectory in a simplified environment and then translate that trajectory into behavior the real task requires.

The method first constructs a paired abstract environment with simpler geometry and physics. Removing difficult dynamics, including physical manipulation, makes trajectories easier to generate. But those trajectories omit details needed for execution, and their individual frames do not line up with the executed motion. A sequence-to-sequence model addresses this mismatch by translating between whole sequences, enabling a low-level policy to follow the abstract plan.

Experiments on unseen long-horizon tasks and different robot embodiments support the practicality of this approach. The contribution is a way to connect easier planning with physically detailed execution despite a substantial gap between them, with experimental evidence for one-shot task generalization.
icml-2023-abstract-to-executable-traject.tldr: Translating simplified plans into executable robot trajectories supports one-shot generalization to unseen long-horizon tasks.

paragraphs: The relational data model was developed to manage and analyze large datasets. This paper asks whether computations written in that model can also be differentiated automatically. The question connects two capabilities: expressing large data computations relationally and obtaining the derivatives needed by machine learning algorithms.

The approach keeps the computation in relational form and runs an automatically differentiated relational algorithm on a relational engine. Its significance lies in bringing differentiation into a computational setting already designed for large-scale data work. The paper therefore examines relational computation as a setting for machine learning execution, extending the role considered for these engines beyond data management and analytics.

The reported experiments show that this combination scales to very large datasets and is competitive with specialized, state-of-the-art systems for distributed machine learning. That is an empirical finding about the evaluated approach, rather than a claim that relational engines always outperform dedicated systems. The result supports the practical viability of automatically differentiated relational algorithms for large-scale learning.
icml-2023-auto-differentiation-of-relati.tldr: Automatically differentiated relational algorithms can scale to very large datasets and compete with specialized distributed machine learning systems.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to release running sums while protecting users through shuffled messages. It introduces multiple concurrent shufflers, each permuting messages from a batch of users. Batches may overlap, and the privacy requirement applies to all shuffled messages taken together, so privacy must hold for the combined output.

For a sequence of length n and k shufflers, the authors give an algorithm whose error scales as n raised to 1/(2k+1), up to logarithmic factors. They also prove a matching lower bound, even when batch sizes can be chosen adaptively. This identifies a precise relationship between the number of concurrent shufflers and achievable accuracy.

With log n shufflers, the error becomes polylogarithmic, improving substantially on the best possible single-shuffler rate of roughly n raised to 1/3. The authors then apply their running-sum algorithm to contextual linear bandits. With sufficiently many shufflers, on the order of log n up to logarithmic factors, they obtain optimal regret of roughly the square root of n.
icml-2023-concurrent-shuffle-differentia.tldr: Concurrent message shufflers provably improve the accuracy of private running sums and enable improved contextual bandit regret.

paragraphs: A bandit algorithm can earn strong total rewards while making some poor individual decisions. This paper studies a stricter requirement: in each round, the selected actions must perform close enough to supplied baseline actions. The setting combines multiple actions per round, action features that change between rounds, and constraints evaluated using only the current round's choices.

The proposed Greedy on Confidence Widths, or GCW, is a meta-algorithm that works with a standard bandit algorithm. It satisfies the round-by-round performance constraints with high probability. If its underlying algorithm has minimax-optimal regret, GCW preserves that optimality up to logarithmic factors, linking conservative behavior to a qualified learning guarantee.

The authors also improve analyses of C²UCB and Thompson sampling for use with GCW. They establish near-optimal regret when feasible action sets are bases of a matroid, a particular combinatorial structure. Experiments on a real-world dataset show performance improving efficiently while the constraints remain satisfied, supporting the practical value of learning under a per-round safeguard.
icml-2023-contextual-conservative-interl.tldr: GCW adds high-probability per-round performance safeguards to bandit learning while preserving near-optimal regret under stated conditions.

paragraphs: When model interactions become part of future training data, today's predictions can influence tomorrow's models. This paper formalizes that feedback process: interactions are recorded as history and later scraped for training. It studies stability by following a prediction bias statistic over time, such as gender bias in model outputs.

The analysis connects bias amplification to whether outputs behave like samples from the training distribution. The authors characterize this property as uniform faithfulness. The distinction matters because a model's way of producing outputs affects the data that subsequent models encounter, and therefore how existing biases evolve through repeated feedback.

Experiments cover image classification, visual role-labeling, and language generation. Models exhibiting more sampling-like behavior are found to be more faithful and more stable in these settings. Building on that relationship, the authors propose an intervention to mitigate and stabilize unstable feedback systems. The findings concern the evolution of bias through feedback; greater stability does not itself establish that the starting distribution is unbiased.
icml-2023-data-feedback-loops-model-driv.tldr: Model outputs that behave more like samples from their training distribution are associated with more stable bias under repeated data feedback.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training examples from an already trained model. This paper addresses deep regression, where models predict numerical values. The authors identify this as a less explored setting than classification or simple linear regression and develop methods specifically for its learning and evaluation requirements.

Their Blindspot method uses a new weight optimization procedure involving two models: a randomly initialized model partially exposed to retained examples, and a copy of the original trained model. Together, these guide the selective preservation of knowledge about retained data and removal of information about examples designated for forgetting. The paper also introduces a Gaussian fine-tuning method.

Because classification unlearning metrics do not transfer directly to regression, the authors adapt those metrics to this setting. Experiments span computer vision, natural language processing, and forecasting. The reported results show strong performance across the evaluated datasets and metrics, including generalization and robustness to privacy attacks. These findings support the proposed methods across several kinds of deep regression application.
icml-2023-deep-regression-unlearning-d9a.tldr: Blindspot and Gaussian fine-tuning extend machine unlearning to deep regression while aiming to retain useful knowledge and resist privacy attacks.

paragraphs: This paper examines what cascaded convolutional decoders can represent by studying their frequency components. Instead of looking only at feature values, the authors apply a discrete Fourier transform to each channel of an intermediate feature map. This exposes how different frequencies behave as information moves through the decoder.

They extend the two-dimensional circular convolution theorem to describe both forward computation and backward learning in the frequency domain. That analysis establishes three defects. Convolution, zero-padding, and several other settings make the decoder more likely to weaken high-frequency components. Upsampling produces spectra in which strong signals recur at particular frequencies, revealing a separate structural effect.

The third result concerns learning a regression mapping: when input and target frequency components have a small shift, the decoder usually cannot be learned effectively. Together, these findings connect specific decoder operations to frequency representation and training difficulties. Their qualifiers matter: the high-frequency result describes a tendency, and the shifted-frequency result describes usual difficulty rather than an unconditional impossibility.
icml-2023-defects-of-convolutional-decod.tldr: Frequency-domain analysis proves three representation defects involving high-frequency weakening, repeated spectral signals, and difficulty learning shifted frequencies.

paragraphs: This paper estimates how treatment effects vary across treated individuals when some confounding factors are unmeasured. It considers balanced panel data, with treatment introduced at the final time point. The method combines difference-in-differences with trees, allowing treatment-effect estimation to respond to differences among groups of observations.

The authors introduce an identification assumption that permits violations of the conditional parallel-trends assumption commonly used in difference-in-differences. Under this replacement assumption, they prove partial identifiability of the conditional average treatment effect on treated individuals. Partial identification is a qualified result: the assumption provides information about the effect without establishing full identification.

Their tree-building rule accounts simultaneously for fit to observed data and violations of conditional parallel trends. It is designed to avoid model misspecification and unnecessary estimation of auxiliary parameters. The authors also combine multiple trees through gradient boosting to enhance performance. Experiments with synthetic and real-world datasets support the method's effectiveness within this setting, connecting a revised identification argument to a practical estimation procedure.
icml-2023-difference-in-differences-meet.tldr: A tree-based difference-in-differences method estimates heterogeneous treatment effects under a new assumption allowing parallel-trend violations and partial identification.

paragraphs: Looking several steps ahead has been useful for evaluating reinforcement learning policies, but its impact on improving policies has been more limited. The authors suggest a possible reason: multi-step policy improvement involves operations that cannot be approximated using stochastic samples. This creates a barrier between the theoretical appeal of looking ahead and practical learning algorithms.

The paper first introduces DoMo-VI, an oracle algorithm that combines multi-step policy improvement with multi-step policy evaluation. It supports general off-policy learning and has a guaranteed convergence speed-up toward the optimal policy. The oracle formulation establishes the theoretical benefit of applying multiple steps to both parts of learning.

DoMo-AC provides a practical actor-critic version of that idea. It introduces a bias-variance trade-off to improve policy-gradient estimates. Combined with the IMPALA architecture, it improves over the baseline algorithm on Atari-57. The abstract thus presents distinct evidence at two levels: a convergence guarantee for DoMo-VI and benchmark improvements for the practical DoMo-AC implementation.
icml-2023-domo-ac-doubly-multi-step-off-.tldr: DoMo-AC turns an oracle approach combining multi-step policy improvement and evaluation into a practical actor-critic method with Atari-57 improvements.

paragraphs: A classifier's confidence is useful when it accurately reflects the probability that its prediction is correct. Deep networks often assign excessive confidence, while focal loss, a proposed remedy, can push predictions toward insufficient confidence. This paper targets the difficulty of balancing those two kinds of calibration error during training.

The proposed dual focal loss uses two logits, the scores involved in forming class predictions. It considers the ground-truth logit together with the highest logit ranked after it. By maximizing the gap between this pair, the method changes how training shapes confidence. The authors argue that this can produce a better balance between overconfidence and underconfidence.

The paper supplies theoretical evidence for the approach and evaluates it across multiple models and datasets, reporting state-of-the-art performance in those evaluations. Its contribution is a training loss explicitly designed around the interaction of two scores. The stated outcome is improved calibration performance in the tested settings, supporting the value of addressing both confidence extremes together.
icml-2023-dual-focal-loss-for-calibratio.tldr: Dual focal loss uses a pair of logits to better balance overconfidence and underconfidence, improving calibration in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Training deep Boltzmann machines requires estimating gradients, and biased estimates are a central difficulty. An existing unbiased approach couples Gibbs-sampling processes, but convergence can be slow in high-dimensional states. This paper changes both the sampling mechanism used for coupling and where the process begins to make unbiased training more efficient.

The method uses Metropolis-Hastings coupling and initializes states near a local mode of the target distribution. The authors exploit the sampler's tendency to reject proposals: in this construction, coupling tends to converge in a single step with high probability. That behavior supplies the efficiency advantage described in the abstract.

The resulting algorithm allows end-to-end training without greedy pretraining. The authors also introduce practical techniques to improve model performance. Their experiments show generative performance comparable to other deep generative models, including an FID score of 10.33 on MNIST. The contribution connects a more efficient unbiased gradient-estimation procedure to a workable training strategy and demonstrated generation quality.
icml-2023-end-to-end-training-of-deep-bo.tldr: Metropolis-Hastings coupling initialized near local modes enables efficient unbiased gradient estimation and end-to-end deep Boltzmann machine training.

paragraphs: Predicting performance on unseen data usually relies on a validation set. Without one, useful generalization bounds are difficult to obtain. This paper pursues the weaker goal of finding a measure that varies monotonically with generalization error, so it can indicate relative generalization behavior without requiring an additional validation dataset.

The proposed REF Complexity compares how a model and training algorithm fit signal versus noise. The motivating intuition is that a combination may generalize well when it learns true labels quickly but random labels slowly. This makes the contrast between two kinds of fitting behavior central to the measure, rather than fitting performance alone.

Experiments report monotonic relationships with test accuracy, including correlations of -0.988 on CIFAR-10 and -0.960 on CIFAR-100. The authors also theoretically support the measure in three settings: convex, smooth optimization with stochastic gradient descent; smooth, potentially nonconvex optimization with stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics; and linear models with gradient descent. These results support its utility under specified regimes without turning an empirical correlation into a universal performance guarantee.
icml-2023-finding-generalization-measure.tldr: REF Complexity contrasts learning signal with fitting noise to measure generalization without an additional validation set.

paragraphs: Neurosymbolic programs combine continuous neural computation with discrete symbolic operations. Learning such programs involves deciding both how to interpret continuous input and how symbolic processing should act on the resulting abstractions. This paper develops a collection of techniques for searching over that mixed kind of program.

The authors relax the discrete and continuous optimization problem so that all modules can be learned jointly through gradient descent. Their toolbox also includes amortized inference, overparameterization, and a differentiable penalty for lengthy programs. Making the length penalty differentiable allows the preference for shorter programs to participate in the same gradient-guided learning process.

Taken together, these techniques improve the stability of gradient-guided program search. The stated significance extends to learning the connection between perception and symbolic computation: how continuous inputs can become discrete abstractions, and how code can process those abstractions. The abstract presents these capabilities as directions suggested by the toolbox, while its direct finding is improved stability of the search process.
icml-2023-from-perception-to-programs-re.tldr: A differentiable toolbox improves the stability of searching for programs that combine neural perception with symbolic computation.

paragraphs: High-quality diffusion-model samples leave open the question of how much uncertainty to attach to their outputs. This paper focuses on image-to-image regression and builds on conformal prediction, which provides finite-sample, distribution-free uncertainty guarantees. The aim is to attach calibrated intervals to individual entries of future generated images.

The authors generalize Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets into a procedure called K-RCPS. It controls a specified notion of risk relative to a ground-truth image while minimizing mean interval length. This pairing matters because uncertainty intervals should satisfy the intended risk requirement while remaining as informative as the optimization permits.

The main technical ingredient is a convex optimization approach that supports multidimensional risk control and provably minimizes mean interval length. The authors demonstrate it on denoising natural face images and abdominal CT scans, reporting state-of-the-art performance. The guarantee concerns the defined risk and calibrated intervals for the image task; the contribution makes that uncertainty objective explicit and optimizable for diffusion-model outputs.
icml-2023-how-to-trust-your-diffusion-mo.tldr: K-RCPS uses convex optimization to construct calibrated image intervals that control a specified risk while minimizing average interval length.

paragraphs: Large pretrained models can perform tasks through prompts without task-specific examples, yet adapting them commonly requires labeled data. POUF addresses adaptation when only unlabeled target data are available. Its framework can fine-tune either the model itself or its prompt, providing two ways to adjust the pretrained system to a downstream task.

The method aligns discrete distributions extracted from prompts and target data. This alignment supplies the basis for adaptation without target labels. The authors show how to apply the framework to both language-augmented vision models and masked-language models, making the same broad approach relevant to visual and language prediction.

Evaluation covers image classification, sentiment analysis, and natural language inference, spanning 13 image-related and 15 language-related tasks. POUF consistently improves over the baselines in these experiments. These findings support the usefulness of distribution alignment for unsupervised adaptation across the evaluated tasks, while preserving the distinction between having zero-shot capabilities and benefiting from further training on unlabeled target data.
icml-2023-pouf-prompt-oriented-unsupervi.tldr: POUF adapts pretrained models or prompts to unlabeled target data by aligning prompt-derived and data-derived distributions.

paragraphs: Models can lose robustness when deployment data differ from their training data. Invariant learning addresses this by trying to distinguish reliable features from spurious ones and learning from the reliable features. Many methods require environment labels or prior information about domains, which the authors identify as difficult to obtain in practice.

TIVA removes the requirement for environment-specific information in the training data. It learns a policy for partitioning environments using attributes independent of the targets, then performs invariant risk minimization. The authors prove that this strategy is possible under certain mild data conditions. The independence requirement and data conditions are part of the stated theoretical result.

Experiments on multiple benchmarks show better performance than the compared baselines and strong robustness under distribution shift. The contribution is therefore both methodological and conditional: it supplies a way to learn the partitions needed for invariant learning, along with a proof under stated conditions and empirical support for the resulting approach.
icml-2023-provably-invariant-learning-wi.tldr: TIVA learns environment partitions without supplied domain information and supports invariant learning under stated data conditions.

paragraphs: Gaussian process upper confidence bound is an approach to optimizing functions treated as black boxes. Its confidence parameter influences exploration, but theoretical prescriptions can be very large, while practical implementations often choose it heuristically. Randomized GP-UCB addresses this tension by drawing the parameter from a Gamma distribution rather than fixing it manually.

This paper first broadens the regret analysis to cover more distributions, including Gamma distributions. It then introduces improved randomized GP-UCB, or IRGP-UCB, using a two-parameter exponential distribution. The resulting method has tighter Bayesian regret bounds, strengthening the theoretical account of performance for this randomized exploration strategy.

A key property is that IRGP-UCB does not require the confidence parameter to increase with the number of optimization iterations. This avoids the later-stage over-exploration associated with that increase. Extensive experiments demonstrate the method's effectiveness. Together, the analysis and experiments support a more controlled randomized choice of exploration strength, with the improvement expressed specifically through Bayesian regret bounds.
icml-2023-randomized-gaussian-process-up.tldr: IRGP-UCB randomizes confidence using a two-parameter exponential distribution to tighten Bayesian regret bounds without increasing exploration over time.

paragraphs: Double-oracle methods combined with regret minimization have shown fast convergence toward Nash equilibrium in games. This paper develops a unified framework for analyzing their convergence rates and sample requirements. It covers both normal-form methods and extensive-form methods, which represent games with sequential decisions and information sets.

Within this framework, the authors extend online double oracle to extensive-form games and determine its sample complexity. They also identify a potential problem with extensive-form double oracle: its sample complexity can grow exponentially with the number of information sets because its stopping threshold for restricted games decreases exponentially.

The proposed Periodic Double Oracle addresses that issue with sample complexity polynomial in the number of information sets. The authors report the lowest sample complexity among regret-minimizing double-oracle methods. Experiments on poker and board games show substantially faster convergence than previous double-oracle algorithms and performance competitive with state-of-the-art regret-minimization methods. The theoretical and empirical results together motivate changing how the restricted-game solving process is organized.
icml-2023-regret-minimizing-double-oracl.tldr: Periodic Double Oracle achieves polynomial sample complexity and faster empirical convergence after analysis exposes a possible exponential cost in XDO.

paragraphs: Some environments change in ways that depend on earlier interactions, so a fixed context does not adequately describe them. This paper introduces Dynamic Contextual Markov Decision Processes to represent contexts that evolve over time. The framework extends contextual MDPs to history-dependent environments whose behavior is non-Markovian.

The authors focus on a special case called logistic DCMDPs. Aggregation functions determine context transitions, allowing this structure to avoid exponential dependence on history length. They use it to derive an algorithm based on upper confidence bounds and establish regret bounds. The tractability result is tied to this structured special case.

Guided by the theory, the paper also introduces a practical model-based algorithm that plans in a latent space and uses optimism over history-dependent features. A recommendation task using MovieLens data demonstrates its effectiveness when user behavior evolves in response to recommendations. This links the formal model to a setting where actions influence both immediate outcomes and the context of later decisions.
icml-2023-reinforcement-learning-with-hi.tldr: Dynamic contextual MDPs model evolving, history-dependent environments, with tractable learning guarantees and a practical algorithm for a structured logistic case.

paragraphs: An explanation can be unstable under adversarial perturbations, raising questions about how reliably it describes a model. This paper asks when explanation robustness requires additional intervention and what that intervention costs. It proves that explanation robustness is determined by the robustness of the model being explained, making robust explanations available for a robust model.

For a non-robust model, the authors prove that composing it with a kernel produces strictly more robust explanations. However, this improvement can introduce a trade-off with faithfulness: an explanation may become more stable while describing the original model less accurately. Robustness and faithfulness therefore need to be assessed as separate properties.

The authors argue that this trade-off can apply to any model and theoretically establish its existence for SmoothGrad. Experiments involving six explanation methods and four backbones support the theoretical findings. The result does not say that every robustness improvement necessarily reduces faithfulness; it establishes that greater robustness can carry that cost, challenging the expectation that stabilizing explanations is automatically beneficial.
icml-2023-robust-explanation-for-free-or.tldr: Explanation robustness depends on model robustness, and making explanations more robust can reduce their faithfulness to the model.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning predicts values in reinforcement learning, and its accuracy depends on how states are represented. When training updates the representation together with the value predictor, those representations change over time. This paper analyzes that evolution to understand what end-to-end TD learning does to the features supporting its predictions.

The first result shows that value approximation error strictly decreases over time when the environment is reversible. Under additional environmental assumptions, the authors connect representation dynamics to a spectral decomposition of the transition matrix. This links the features learned during training to structure in how the environment moves between states.

That second result motivates an auxiliary task: learning multiple value functions associated with randomly generated rewards. The authors empirically validate its usefulness for representation learning in tabular environments and Atari games. The guarantees remain tied to their respective assumptions, while the experiments support the practical value of using several random-reward prediction tasks to help learn state representations.
icml-2023-towards-a-better-understanding.tldr: Conditional analysis links TD representation learning to transition structure and motivates useful auxiliary predictions of values under random rewards.

paragraphs: Preferential Bayesian optimization learns from comparisons between pairs of choices, called duels, when reliable numerical feedback is unavailable. A Gaussian-process preference model can express flexible preferences, but its posterior is a computationally difficult skew Gaussian process. Common Gaussian approximations simplify that posterior by ignoring its skewness.

The authors examine those approximations and find that predicted duel probabilities can be inaccurate. They then improve Monte Carlo estimation for the skew posterior, demonstrating the practical efficiency of Gibbs sampling and deriving an estimator with low variance. These changes address posterior estimation while preserving the preference structure that motivates using the skew model.

Even with these improvements, Markov chain Monte Carlo can remain a computational bottleneck. The paper therefore develops another method intended to combine efficient computation with low sample complexity, and extensive numerical experiments demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution addresses two connected practical concerns: the accuracy of predictions used to choose comparisons and the computational cost of obtaining those predictions.
icml-2023-towards-practical-preferential.tldr: The paper improves skew-Gaussian preference inference and develops a practical optimization method after finding inaccuracies in Gaussian duel predictions.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks perform well on graph-structured data, but explaining that success theoretically remains challenging. This paper studies their generalization gap: the difference between training performance and performance on the prediction targets of interest. It approaches the question while explicitly accounting for stochastic optimization, connecting training behavior with generalization analysis.

The authors first establish high-probability bounds on the generalization gap and gradients for transductive learning algorithms. They then develop high-probability generalization-gap bounds for popular graph neural networks. This progression connects a broader analysis of learning algorithms to the specific network families being studied.

The resulting theory identifies how network architecture affects the generalization gap and analyzes factors influencing generalization capability. Experiments on benchmark datasets support the theoretical findings. The contribution is an account of architectural influence through probabilistic bounds, backed by empirical validation. It helps explain why the design of a graph neural network matters for generalization within the transductive setting considered by the paper.
icml-2023-towards-understanding-generali.tldr: High-probability generalization bounds connect graph neural network architecture and stochastic training to generalization in transductive learning.

paragraphs: Self-predictive learning builds representations by predicting their own future values. This creates a troubling possibility: a constant representation can be perfectly predictable while carrying no useful information. The paper studies why successful learning can avoid that collapse, focusing on how the optimization process shapes representations rather than only on the prediction objective.

The authors identify two crucial design choices: optimizing the predictor at a faster pace and using semi-gradient updates for the representation. In an idealized setting, they show that the resulting dynamics perform a spectral decomposition of the state transition matrix. This explains how self-prediction can capture information about environmental transitions.

Those insights motivate bidirectional self-predictive learning, which learns two representations simultaneously. Small-scale experiments examine the robustness of the theoretical insights, and large-scale experiments demonstrate the new algorithm's promise. The spectral explanation is explicitly tied to the idealized setup, while the empirical work explores the usefulness of the underlying optimization choices and the proposed learning method.
icml-2023-understanding-self-predictive-.tldr: Carefully designed optimization helps self-predictive representations avoid collapse and motivates a bidirectional reinforcement learning representation method.

paragraphs: The advantage function is important for improving a reinforcement learning policy, yet it is often obtained indirectly from a learned Q-function. This paper asks whether learning advantage directly would be more effective. Its proposed VA-learning method learns both the advantage function and the value function without explicitly referring to Q-functions.

VA-learning uses bootstrapping, so its learning updates depend on existing estimates, and it supports off-policy learning. The authors establish theoretical guarantees similar to those of Q-learning. This provides a theoretical basis for changing which quantities the algorithm learns directly, while retaining guarantees comparable to the established approach.

Experiments show improved sample efficiency over Q-learning in both tabular implementations and deep reinforcement learning agents on Atari-57. The paper also identifies a close connection to the dueling architecture. That connection partially explains why the architectural change can improve DQN performance. Together, the results support direct value-and-advantage learning as an efficient alternative in the evaluated settings and clarify part of an existing architectural benefit.
icml-2023-va-learning-as-a-more-efficien.tldr: VA-learning directly learns values and advantages, with Q-learning-like guarantees and improved sample efficiency in tabular and Atari-57 experiments.
